item.title: E-40 Backs Valkyries As Too $hort & LaRussell Join WNBA Finals
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: E-40 backed the Valkyries on Instagram as Too $hort and LaRussell prepared to bring Bay Area rap to Game 2 of the WNBA Finals.
item.content:encoded:
E-40 backed the Golden State Valkyries on Instagram ahead of the WNBA Finals, while Too $hort and LaRussell prepared to join the team’s title run. The two rappers have roles in Game 2 on Monday night at Chase Center.

Last week, E-40 shared a reel with the Valkyries and Chase Center. The black-and-white clip mixed game footage with a courtside shot of the rapper. He exchanged a fist bump near the court.

“Tell us when to go. The Finals start tomorrow. See you there, Yay Area,” the caption read.

View this post on Instagram

E-40 also attended Golden State’s October 9 win over the Aces in Las Vegas, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. The win clinched a Finals berth for a team in just its second year.

Too $hort has made the team part of his playoff plans, too. He praised its fans in a Sports Illustrated interview published after Saturday’s opener. He put the noise at Chase Center above the crowds at Warriors games.

“They’re not lying, like Ballhalla is louder. The fans are more intense,” he told the outlet.

E-40’s caption played off “Tell Me When To Go,” his 2006 track with Keak da Sneak.

Too $hort’s role has gone beyond hearing his own hits in the stands. He played halftime at Golden State’s first home playoff game in September. He has gone to every home playoff game since, Sports Illustrated reported.

For Monday’s Game 2, the San Francisco Chronicle reported that Too $hort was set to handle the pregame drum. Vallejo’s LaRussell was booked for halftime. Larry June played that slot at Saturday’s opener.

The three rappers share roots in the Bay’s sound. AllHipHop covered their roles in the 2023 podcast series “Remember the Time: The Hyphy Movement.” It traced the music, dance, slang and car culture that shaped the scene.

The Finals also changed the city’s rap calendar. Chase Center moved Doja Cat’s show with Latto from October 19 to October 25. The venue’s event page tied the move to Golden State’s Finals berth.

The Valkyries enter Game 2 up 1-0. They beat the Atlanta Dream 68-64 on October 17, led by Gabby Williams’ 26 points. The team’s official preview lists Monday’s tipoff at 5 P.M. Pacific, or 8 P.M. Eastern. USA Network and Peacock will carry the game.

item.title: Cardi B Wanted Crab Cakes, Got Carrots At NPR’s “Tiny Desk”
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Cardi B joked about missing crab cakes and getting vegetables as she brought her catalog hits to NPR's intimate performance series.
item.content:encoded:
Cardi B wanted crab cakes at NPR’s “Tiny Desk.” She said she got celery and carrots, then took the set into “I Like It.”

The performance premiered Monday on NPR Music’s official YouTube channel. The video ran 18 minutes and 46 seconds.

Cardi aired her food complaint after “Bodak Yellow.” Chicken wings, crab cakes and blue crab all made her list of missing food.

“They got the best crab cakes out here,” she said. Instead, she told the room, she had received “Just celery sticks and carrots.” She also joked about sweating in latex.

Earlier, Cardi moved through “Be Careful” before calling for a shift in mood. “Change the vibes,” she said. Then came “Up,” with its repeated hook and verses. She later reached “Bodak Yellow,” followed by the snack complaint and her closing song.

The smaller setting followed a big year on the road. Pollstar’s midyear report ranked Cardi seventh among the world’s touring acts. Her “Little Miss Drama Tour” grossed $72.1 million. The run traveled through North American arenas from February through April.

By its halfway point, the tour had sold 209,622 tickets across 17 shows and grossed more than $32 million, Pollstar reported. The full trek was scheduled for 35 shows. Two nights at the Forum in Inglewood drew 25,145 fans. Live Nation said she was the first female rapper to sell out two shows there.

The trek also marked a shift in how Cardi toured. Pollstar noted that most of her earlier concert dates in its archives had been festivals or shows with several acts. She had headlined individual arena dates in 2019, but this was her first full arena run.

The tour supported her second album, “Am I the Drama?” It arrived September 19, 2025, through Atlantic Records. It followed her 2018 debut, “Invasion of Privacy,” giving the arena run a second studio album to draw from alongside her older hits. AllHipHop’s earlier coverage tracked the tour announcement just before the album came out.

At “Tiny Desk,” “I Like It” carried the set into its final minutes. A call for applause for the band, singers and audience followed. The video ended with cheers.

item.title: Metro Boomin & Big Sean Join Rolling Loud India’s 2026 Lineup
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Metro Boomin and Big Sean joined Rolling Loud India's December bill, which pairs U.S. stars with Indian acts as venue details await.
item.content:encoded:
Metro Boomin and Big Sean landed spots at Rolling Loud India, joining ScHoolboy Q and GoldLink on the festival’s second-year bill.

The two-day event is set for December 12 and 13, 2026, in Mumbai. The lineup is listed on District’s official event page.

Metro Boomin, Big Sean and GoldLink are on the first day’s bill with Burna Boy. ScHoolboy Q plays the second day, which has Skepta and Karan Aujla at the top. Aujla returns after helping headline the first India edition in 2025.

The bill also brings in Indian acts Dhanda Nyoliwala on day one and Seedhe Maut on day two.

That mix was part of the plan, Rolling Loud co-founder and CEO Matt Zingler said in a statement published by Rolling Stone India.

“One thing that really stood out to us in India was how open the fans were to everything.”

He said that response helped shape a bill built to bring Indian and international acts together across both days.

District CEO Rahul Ganjoo said the team looked at who drew fans to cyphers and small shows when building the bill. He said last year’s crowds stayed for both Indian and international sets.

The names followed earlier date and ticket announcements. The December dates were public by September 10, when the lineup was still under wraps.

Early ticket access through an exclusive HSBC window was scheduled for September 29 and was set to last 48 hours. A general sale was scheduled for October 1. A September 22 report still described Metro Boomin’s name as an online rumor rather than a confirmed booking.

Then the lineup reveal hit a delay. Kharghar News reported on October 14 that organizers had pushed back a planned noon announcement. Their update gave no new reveal date.

Wiz Khalifa and Don Toliver helped lead last year’s bill. This year brings a different set of U.S. names, while Aujla links the new lineup to the debut.

In January, Rolling Loud billed Orlando as its only U.S. festival for 2026, putting the India event among the brand’s overseas dates.

District still lists the Mumbai venue as TBA. Rolling Stone India says more venue and festival schedule information is expected in the coming weeks.

item.title: North West, Ken Carson And Kanye West Caught In Bizarre Fake Dating Scandal
item.dc:creator: illseed
item.description: North West's alleged romance with Ken Carson and Kanye West's supposed allowance threat has unraveled as a whole downer.
item.content:encoded:
Let’s get to busting some rumors. North West is at the center of a wild Ken Carson dating rumor. WTF? I had to do the research on this since Ken is a grown man of 26 years of age. In this one, Kanye West threatened to cut off his daughter’s allowance and all that. But the Internet has decided to lie once again.

According to the viral story, North posted photographs of herself enjoying a yacht excursion with rapper Ken Carson, who was being identified as her boyfriend. That alone should have prompted some serious skepticism. North is 13 years old, while Carson is a grown man.

But whoever concocted this tale apparently decided a questionable romance wasn’t enough. They kept going!

The story continued with Kanye West supposedly discovering the pictures and demanding that his daughter remove them. According to these screenshots, Ye threatened to cut off North’s allowance if she refused to comply. Well…they kept going.

North’s supposed response was that her mother, Kim Kardashian, would simply pay her bills instead. I mean, that seems plausible…and yet we know better than to accept this.

The whole thing appears to be fake. I mean, common sense says it is fugazi!

Tthe viral material on the yacht photograph were manipulated and actually originated from North’s 2025 birthday celebration. In the original photograph, Mama Kim was beside her daughter, not Ken The Man. Some Internet Goob decided to replace Mom with Ken Carson. WILD WORK!

The text messages between Kanye and North have also been identified as fabricated.

Kanye West has certainly generated his share of authentic family controversies – this one is ICK. Glad it is fake. And frankly, dragging a 13-year-old into an invented romantic relationship with an adult rapper crosses a line that should concern everybody. Jeez. I’d like to swing on somebody over this one.

This is precisely why we have Rumor Busters here at AllHipHop.

Sometimes the most sensational story is also the easiest one to manufacture and because these people are definitely “wild and crazy,” we tend to believe anything is possible.

As for North, Kanye and Ken Carson?

There is no yacht romance, no allowance threat and no confrontation.

RUMOR BUSTED!

  • illseed way out!

item.title: Panthers Flip Meek Mill’s “Dreams And Nightmares” To Troll Eagles
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Meek Mill's Eagles anthem became a Panthers punchline after Carolina's 25-14 win, with a "No dreams, just nightmares" taunt.
item.content:encoded:
Meek Mill’s “Dreams and Nightmares” became a Carolina Panthers punchline Sunday, when the team turned the Eagles’ victory anthem into a taunt after beating Philadelphia on its home field.

After beating Philadelphia 25-14 at Lincoln Financial Field, Carolina posted “No dreams, just nightmares” on its official X account alongside an image and a link to game highlights. The line flipped the title of Meek’s 2012 song, which became part of the Eagles’ first Super Bowl championship run.

The Panthers also went after another piece of Philly pride. A separate post pictured quarterback Bryce Young as the Rocky Balboa statue and carried the message, “Yo Adrian, we did it!” ESPN included both posts in its roundup of the weekend’s NFL taunts.

Carolina left Philadelphia with a 3-2 record, while the Eagles fell to 2-4. The music reference gave the score a sting beyond the standings. The Panthers had borrowed a song Eagles players and fans used to celebrate some of their biggest wins, then removed the dreams from it.

That connection reached a national audience in February 2018, when the Eagles entered Super Bowl LII to “Dreams and Nightmares” before facing the New England Patriots. After winning the franchise’s first Super Bowl, players played the song again in their locker room.

The record had already been part of the team’s playoff buildup, including warmups before its NFC championship win over the Minnesota Vikings. Meek was incarcerated during that run, and players’ support for the hometown rapper gave the anthem another layer of meaning beyond getting ready for kickoff.

The Eagles’ bond with the song lasted well beyond that championship. Meek performed it at Lincoln Financial Field before Philadelphia played the Dallas Cowboys in October 2022, bringing the rapper himself into a setting where his record had become familiar.

Then, during the Eagles’ January 2023 NFC championship celebration, “Dreams and Nightmares” played as the team finished its 31-7 win over the San Francisco 49ers. Meek attended that game and turned the celebration into more music, sharing a freestyle over Tupac Shakur’s “Hit Em Up” after the win. He also offered to perform the song at a free party in the city: “I will host a free party tonight and perform intro lol somebody open a club up.”

item.title: Digital Underground’s Money B Reveals The Truth About Tupac, Shock G’s Humpty Hump Struggles & Untold History
item.dc:creator: Chuck Creekmur (@ChuckCreekmur)
item.description: Digital Underground's Money B reveals how Tupac really joined the group, and why Shock G grew frustrated with Humpty Hump's fame.
item.content:encoded:
Money B Tells His Story…

Before Tupac Shakur became one of Hip-Hop’s most influential figures, before “The Humpty Dance” turned Digital Underground into a household name, and before Shock G’s alter ego Humpty Hump became larger than life, there was a collective of young artists in Oakland determined to do something different.

Money B was there for nearly all of it.

Born in Philadelphia and raised in the Bay Area, the veteran MC grew up surrounded by revolutionary politics. Both of his parents were members of the Black Panther Party, and he attended Oakland Community School, where Huey P. Newton personally handed him his graduation certificate.

That foundation would eventually intersect with one of Hip-Hop’s most creative groups and one of its most iconic artists, Tupac Shakur.

Now, with his new book, A D.U. Party Don’t Stop: The Money B Story, Money B is revisiting the triumphs, tensions and unexpected moments that helped shape his extraordinary journey. (Click here to purchase this riveting memoir.)

In this candid conversation with AllHipHop’s Chuck “Jigsaw” Creekmur and DJ Thoro, Money B discusses everything from Tupac’s early days and their shared political upbringing to Shock G’s frustration with Humpty Hump’s popularity. He also addresses an unusual viral photograph of himself with Tupac and recalls the night Digital Underground deliberately got booed at the Apollo Theater.

The Interview

AllHipHop (Chuck Creekmur): Your parents were Black Panthers?

Money B: Yes. Both my mom and my dad joined the Black Panthers at the Philadelphia chapter in 1970, I want to say. Then my dad moved to the Bay like a year or two later. About a year after that, me and my mom followed.

Shortly after, that’s where I attended Oakland Community School.

AllHipHop: What was the difference between that school and a regular public school?

Money B: You were placed in class not by your age, but by your aptitude. However much you were able to learn, you weren’t held back.

Another thing about the school is we were taught how to learn as opposed to being forced what to learn. It was encouraged to ask questions, to be inquisitive.

I probably read Malcolm X when I was like 11. They would teach us about Marcus Garvey, and we knew about Langston Hughes. I actually met Rosa Parks. She came and visited.

AllHipHop: There’s a picture of you and Huey P. Newton in the book. What’s the story?

Money B: That’s when I graduated from Oakland Community School, basically sixth-grade age. Every year, Huey P. would usually be there at the graduation ceremony, and he’d be the one to hand out the diploma.

That’s a picture of Huey P. Newton giving me my certificate of graduation. That’s actually my brother and sister in the picture with me.

DJ Thoro: With that upbringing, was there any conflict when you wanted to get into the music business?

Money B: My father always hoped that I would talk more about pro-Black, socially conscious music because he loved Public Enemy and Paris.

He actually was a consultant on Paris’s video. When Paris came out, he reached out to my dad.

AllHipHop: What was the original concept of Digital Underground before the group became what we knew?

Money B: Originally, Shock wanted Digital Underground to be more like a pro-Black militant group.

But back then, you couldn’t be a biter. Up until Public Enemy came out, it was like, somebody’s doing it. We can’t do that. We couldn’t come out wearing dashikis because the Jungle Brothers were already doing that.

If you really pay close attention, Digital Underground’s music always has an underlying message. We just weren’t over the top with it.

We make you dance, want you to have fun, party, kick it with us, but also learn a little something along the way.

Shock’s main message, at least the way I interpreted it, was about unity and bringing everybody together.

AllHipHop: How did you and Shock G actually meet?

Money B: Digital Underground put a record out in 1988 called “Underwater Rimes.” At that time, it was just Shock and Chopmaster J.

They needed a DJ. DJ Fuze was recognized as probably one of the hottest DJs in the Bay, and me and Fuze were a group called Raw Fusion.

They came to the crib, and Fuze was renting a room in my mom’s apartment. So I’m there with these guys coming to take my DJ!

After the meeting, Fuze agreed to work with them, but only under the condition that they work with us. We’re a group. We’re not breaking up.

AllHipHop: Digital Underground eventually became a huge collective.

Money B: It definitely was a collective. Everybody came in with the understanding that the goal was for everybody to get their own deal and project.

We were literally Wu-Tang before Wu-Tang.

When Pac came aboard, he was a solo artist. Me and Fuze were Raw Fusion before we got in the group, knowing this was going to help us get a deal for a Raw Fusion album, a Tupac album, Saafir and everybody else.

AllHipHop: How did Tupac come into the group? Was he trying to get down with you guys?

Money B: No, that’s not how it happened.

He was a solo artist signed to TNT Records, which was the label we were signed to.

Before he was a solo artist, he was in a group called Strictly Dope with Ray Luv. They were working on their demo, so they were around us.

Pac and I were close to the same age. When he used to come to Oakland, my house was the hangout house. Me and Fuze had the equipment, turntables, records, and my block was active. Pac liked that.

It got to a point where I think Atron feared he might lose him because it was taking too long, in Tupac’s opinion, for him to get a deal.

We were about to go on our first U.S. tour, and Atron asked if we could bring him.

Everybody likes to say he was a dancer. His job description was just to come and help us with whatever we needed help with.

It could be dancing, helping break down equipment, all these things we all did. He wasn’t just a roadie. He would rhyme, sometimes be the hype man. We all had roles.

AllHipHop: Did you and Pac connect as Panther Cubs, since both your parents were Black Panthers?

Money B: Yes and no.

We didn’t sit around and have meetings about how we were going to take down the white man. We didn’t do that.

But because we had similar upbringings, when he would talk about what people thought were radical thoughts, his messaging was never foreign to me.

When he mentioned political prisoners, Geronimo Pratt and Assata Shakur, I knew who these people were.

He didn’t have to explain anything to me. I think there was probably some comfort in that.

It was unspoken.

AllHipHop: Let’s talk about Humpty Hump. Did he eventually become bigger than Digital Underground?

Money B: He became the star. There became a point where Humpty was bigger than the entire group.

More importantly, he was bigger than Shock G, but Shock G was the one who created him.

Shock openly admitted that some chicks would want him to put the nose on!

He told us the first time Humpty Hump really got busy. Shock G didn’t get it. Humpty got it!

But Shock was such a great musician, and he wanted to be recognized for that.

At one point, he felt like all people wanted was Humpty. He wasn’t trying to kill Humpty, but he wasn’t excited to keep doing it.

I think The Body-Hat Syndrome album was a way to go in the opposite direction because Tommy Boy wanted more Humpty pop songs.

He didn’t want to give them another Humpty hit because then he would be pigeonholed forever.

AllHipHop (DJ Thoro): I was at the Apollo when you guys came out with bags over your heads and everybody started booing. Who planned that?

Money B: We were at rehearsal, goofing around. I think Pee Wee came up with the idea because of the Unknown Comic from The Gong Show.

Shock was like, “No, let’s really do that.”

But the only way it would work was if we got booed. We had to think of the wackest everything to make sure we got booed.

We couldn’t let production know. The Sandman didn’t know. Kiki Shepard didn’t know. Mark Curry didn’t know.

Mark’s from Oakland, and I knew him. If I had said something, he would have recognized my voice.

When we revealed ourselves, they went crazy. New York love was crazy!

AllHipHop: There’s also that picture of you and Tupac that people keep talking about. Can you clarify it?

Money B: I get it. If I was a friend of that person in that situation, I’d be cracking on them.

But back then, if you were on the road, the only person who had their own room was the star, which was Shock.

Other than that, me and Pac were roommates. Fuze and Money? Everybody had a roommate.

Obviously, he sat down and took a picture. I don’t know what else you want me to say.

Other than that, you’re implying something, and if you know me, it’s ridiculous. If you don’t know me, that’s fine, too.

AllHipHop: Nothing to see here?

Money B: Nothing to see.

Editor’s note: The interview has been condensed and lightly edited for clarity. The final exchange refers to Money B and Tupac sharing a room while touring, with other group members also assigned roommates.

item.title: Young Miko Sells Out Intuit Dome On Her First Arena Tour
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Young Miko sold out her first Intuit Dome show and thanked fans as her first arena tour brought her growing audience to Los Angeles.
item.content:encoded:
Young Miko sold out her first show at Inglewood’s Intuit Dome, adding a Los Angeles-area milestone to the arena tour she launched after opening for Billie Eilish last year.

The Puerto Rican rapper grew emotional during Saturday’s concert as she took in the crowd. Destin Conrad joined her for “no debo :(,” giving the night a guest appearance from the singer featured on her “Do Not Disturb: Late Checkout” project.

“Today I have more people than ever before and I can’t thank you enough for the support you’ve given me,” she told the crowd in Spanish, as translated by The Hollywood Reporter.

The sellout came during her first global headlining arena tour. Her path to that run included eight opening dates on Eilish’s “Hit Me Hard And Soft Tour” in 2025, with stops in markets including New York, Philadelphia and Orlando.

She then moved into headlining arenas in Puerto Rico that same year. Her first show at the Coliseo de Puerto Rico sold out in 90 minutes, prompting a second date that also sold out, tour promoter Live Nation said. Those hometown shows preceded the broader arena run now reaching U.S. cities.

The announced U.S. arena schedule placed Seattle first on October 13, followed by San Francisco two days later. Los Angeles was the third date on that leg, before the route headed toward the Southwest.

That expansion has come alongside a bigger presence beyond her own concerts. Young Miko appeared in Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl halftime show earlier this year. In March, Gap built its “Sweats Like This” campaign around a new version of her “WASSUP” video, bringing her music into a global fashion rollout.

Saturday’s show started more than an hour after the venue’s listed 8 P.M. showtime, THR reported. The crowd greeted Young Miko loudly when she arrived onstage, and she closed the night with “WASSUP.”

The “Late Checkout Tour” was announced with 31 dates across 11 countries. Its remaining U.S. itinerary includes San Antonio’s Freeman Coliseum on October 22 and Houston’s Toyota Center on October 24, with the final announced stop at Brooklyn’s Barclays Center on November 5.

item.title: Rapsody Pushes Back On Christian Rapper Label
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Rapsody rejected the Christian rapper label and explained how faith, politics and personal freedom shaped her latest music.
item.content:encoded:
Rapsody rejected the Christian-rapper label while explaining why the faith running through “God Gotta Afro & Gold Hoops” should not define the limits of her music.

“I do not consider myself a Christian rapper. I don’t like labels at all. I’m just a truth teller,” she told NPR.

The North Carolina MC said her songs made room for God alongside politics and everyday life. In the new interview, she also described the strain of trying to meet mainstream expectations about how women in Hip-Hop should look and what their music should sound like.

Her fifth album, released in August, reflected a period when she felt freer to follow her own interests. Its title was not meant to lock God into one appearance, she explained. Instead, she wanted listeners to recognize themselves in the divine and consider a presence beyond any single image.

That refusal to accept a narrow category has a history. In 2024, Rapsody pushed back against separating “female” Hip-Hop from the rest of the culture. Her latest comments extended that argument to the religious themes in her work.

The album also grew out of a journey through Ghana and South Africa. Rapsody previously explained that an Afrofuturism exhibition at the Smithsonian helped spark questions about Black identity and ancestry. She traveled to Ghana, visited historical sites and later recorded much of the project in Johannesburg.

Those experiences shaped a record concerned with preserving Black culture as well as exploring belief. During an August conversation with TIDAL, she described approaching the album as something future listeners could discover and learn from, carrying a record of Black experiences that might otherwise be lost.

That aim also informed the guests she brought into the music. Producer Mr. Porter suggested reaching out to George Clinton, who appeared on “OMG! (Love to Sun Ra).” Rapsody explained that working with an elder offered a chance to listen and learn while keeping cultural knowledge alive.

She had already made clear that her vision left room for women with very different styles. Speaking with Rolling Stone Africa in June, she put it this way: “There is a place for all of it.”

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Madlib Can’t Shake Egon As Catalog Fight Survives
item.dc:creator: Grouchy Greg Watkins (@GrouchyGreg)
item.description: Madlib lost his bid to end Egon’s catalog case as a judge kept the music-rights fight alive and ordered him to answer.
item.content:encoded:
Madlib failed to shut down Egon’s federal catalog lawsuit on October 15, keeping a fight over the right to use years of his recordings in court.

U.S. Magistrate Judge John D. Early denied a motion from Madlib, whose legal name is Otis Jackson Jr., to dismiss the amended case brought by former manager Eothen “Egon” Alapatt. The judge gave Madlib 14 days to answer.

Egon claims their shared company, Madicine Show, holds an implied, nonexclusive license to use the music. His case asks the court to find that Madlib could not simply revoke those rights.

The ruling lets Egon try to prove that claim. It does not settle who owns the recordings.

Egon says the pair never set an end date for the licenses. Madlib argued that the rights ended when a state court dissolved the company. Early rejected that as a basis to throw out the case.

“The Court herein does not decide how a state court receiver should assign rights in the alleged licenses. However, Plaintiff’s alleged copyright license is not extinguished under the Copyright Act merely because Madicine Show has dissolved, as discussed in the Rule 12(b)(6) discussion below,” Early wrote.

The order also names Piñata, Freddie Gibbs and Madlib’s 2014 joint album. Early declined to consider a disputed copyright registration for the album because he did not need it to rule.

In a May 2013 interview, Egon told Dust & Grooves that Madlib Invazion ran their shared label, tours and production work. He said they released 13 albums through the Madlib Medicine Show series.

The fight grew out of Madlib’s October 2024 state lawsuit. He accused Egon of self-dealing, poor management and blocking access to business records.

A state judge appointed a receiver to wind up Madicine Show on October 10, 2025. Egon filed the federal case the next month, as AllHipHop previously reported.

Madlib argued that a federal ruling would intrude on the state receiver’s control. Early disagreed, finding that the court could rule on the parties’ rights without taking the recordings from the receiver.

The judge also drew a line between a license’s existence and whether someone can transfer it.

“The Court may, in the context of an action for declaratory relief, determine whether Plaintiff has a valid license in the Recordings under the Copyright Act without deciding whether Plaintiff may transfer that license to others,” Early wrote.

Early found that the case raised a federal copyright issue and could proceed now. Madlib can still offer evidence that the parties meant the licenses to end with the company. For now, the judge ordered him to answer Egon’s amended complaint within 14 days of the October 15 order.

item.title: Nino Paid & Warhol.SS Face Felony Murder Charges In Atlanta Killing
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Nino Paid and Warhol.SS faced felony murder charges after Atlanta police linked them to a fatal April shooting.
item.content:encoded:
Nino Paid and Warhol.SS were charged with felony murder, armed robbery and aggravated assault in connection with a fatal April shooting in Atlanta.

Atlanta police named Jacquawn Andrews and Zahair Myles as the suspects in a September 15 announcement. Pitchfork identified them as Nino Paid and Warhol.SS, respectively, in its October 15 report.

“Following a thorough investigation, investigators identified two suspects, Zahair Myles and Jacquawn Andrews, in connection with the incident,” police said.

Warhol.SS also faced a charge of criminal attempt to commit a felony. The police announcement listed that charge separately but did not explain which felony investigators believed he had attempted.

Officers responded to 633 Boulevard NE in Atlanta’s Old Fourth Ward around 4:29 A.M. on April 25. They found a 29-year-old man who had been shot several times. He was taken to a local hospital in critical but stable condition and later died, according to police.

The Homicide Unit also responded because of the man’s severe injuries, police said. The police announcement did not explain how the robbery charge related to the fatal encounter.

Border Patrol arrested Nino Paid September 1 as he tried to re-enter the United States from Canada. The department’s September 15 announcement said he was being held in Michigan pending extradition to Georgia. Warhol.SS surrendered September 14 and was booked into Fulton County Jail.

Pitchfork identified the victim as Keion Borders. It also reported that Ring doorbell footage helped identify Nino Paid as an alleged accomplice. The police announcement did not describe that footage or say who allegedly fired the shots.

Warhol.SS declined to comment when Pitchfork contacted representatives for both rappers. The outlet listed an October 15 bond hearing for Nino Paid but did not report an outcome.

The artists had a musical connection before the arrests. They released their joint single “5 STAR B*TCH” on April 4, 2025. Nino Paid released “Somewhere Over The Rainbow” on August 4, less than a month before police arrested him at the border.

The charges are allegations, not findings of guilt. Both men are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. The September police statement did not give a motive for the shooting.
